title.zh: 唱着轻柔水歌的鹅卵石池洞
title.en: The Pebble-Pool Cave Where Water Sings Soft

content:
从前，在柳风森林的最深处——那里的树儿都弯下腰，轻轻对着微风说悄悄话，萤火虫像慢悠悠的金色小星星，飘来飘去——住着一个名叫艾拉的小孩子。艾拉穿着一双软乎乎的羊毛袜子，一只脚趾是蓝色的，另一只脚趾是绿色的；她还挎着一个小布包，上面用线细细缝着几朵小白雏菊。她从不着急跑，也从不大声喊叫。她最喜欢那些安静的时刻——雨点与雨点之间那一小会儿的静默，一只猫咪睡着时轻轻呼出的一口气，还有傍晚临睡前，阳光斜斜照进来，光柱里那些小灰尘跳起的轻盈舞蹈。

一天傍晚，天空变成了暖暖的蜂蜜色，蟋蟀们开始哼起轻柔又平稳的小调，艾拉踩着一条由青苔石头和害羞紫罗兰铺成的小路，慢慢往前走。小路弯弯曲曲地往下延伸，像一条困了的小河，正慢悠悠地往家游呢。她光着的小脚丫踩在泥土上，凉凉的；踩在光滑的小石子上，滑滑的；踩在毛茸茸的青苔上，软软的——全都像小猫耳朵一样温柔。

然后——哎呀！——她听见了。

一个像水在哼摇篮曲的声音。

不大声，也不着急，只是“嘘——嗡……嘘——嗡……”，像呼吸，像泡泡，像一首从梦里刚想起来一半的歌。

艾拉停下脚步，歪着小脑袋听了听。一只小瓢虫飞过来，轻轻停在她的鼻尖上，一动不动，细细的小腿儿痒痒地挠着她，翅膀收得整整齐齐，像一块叠好的丝绸。

声音是从一帘垂柳枝后面传来的——长长的、细细的柳叶垂得低低的，轻轻扫着地面，像绿色的手指。艾拉轻轻把柳条分开，一点点、再一点点，然后踮着脚，走了进去。

就在山坡边上，像大地悄悄藏起来的一个小秘密，出现了一个山洞。

可这可不是黑漆漆、阴森森的山洞——完全不是哦！

这个山洞张开大大的、暖暖的怀抱，洞口一圈是圆溜溜、滑溜溜的石头，被时间跟流水磨得又软又亮。阳光还照得进来，暖暖的、金灿灿的，正好洒在洞中央那一小汪水池上，闪着细细碎碎的光。这水池啊，还没一个汤碗大——可它居然会唱歌呢！

唱歌的不是池子里的水，而是掉进水池里的水。

从高高的岩壁上，一道细细的、银亮亮的水线悄悄滑下来——真的只是一小股细细的水流，像一条清凉透明的光带。水滴落下来的时候，正好敲在岩壁边一颗小小的、圆圆的、完美的鹅卵石上。

“叮。”

又一滴水落下来。

“咚。”

再一滴。

“叮……咚……叮……”

每一滴水都落得刚刚好，轻轻敲在石头上，像一只小小的手指，敲着一面小小的鼓。而那颗石头——光滑的灰石头上，还带着一点点粉红色的水晶斑点——就轻轻回了一声，一个圆润、柔软的音符。不尖，不响，就是暖暖的，像声音给的一个拥抱。

艾拉盘着腿，坐在软软的青苔地上，小雏菊布包放在身边。她看着水滴落下，看着石头接住每一滴水，看着水波一圈圈荡开——小小的圆圈，一个套着一个，不着急，也不停下。

一只白蛾子扑棱棱飞进来，翅膀像一张折好的旧纸，轻轻停在水池边。它不喝水，就那么静静歇着，翅膀一起一伏，节奏和水的歌声一模一样，轻轻的，柔柔的。

艾拉闭上了眼睛。

她听见“叮咚、叮咚”的声音，像心跳——慢一点，稳一点，一直都在那儿。

她感觉到山洞暖暖地围着她，就像裹在一条安静的、厚厚的棉被里。

她闻到湿漉漉的石头味，洞口旁边野薄荷的清香，还有林下草那一点点淡淡的、甜甜的、绿绿的、让人想打个哈欠的味道。

她想起奶奶的手，在撒满面粉的桌子上揉面团。  
她想起夕阳西下时，云朵变得软软的，变成桃子粉、薰衣草紫。  
她想起自己平躺在三叶草地上看天空时，呼吸慢慢变慢，天色也一点点从蓝，变成温柔的暮色玫瑰粉。

在山洞里，时间不会“嘀嗒嘀嗒”走，也不会飞快奔跑。它只是——发着光。像阳光底下放着的一罐蜂蜜。

艾拉伸出手——不是去碰水，也不是去动石头——只是把手轻轻放在水池边，那儿正升腾起一缕缕软软的、银亮亮的水雾。雾气绕着她的手指转了转，凉凉的，柔柔的，又像一句悄悄话，轻轻散开了。

一只知更鸟跳到洞口，歪着头看了看。它没唱歌，只是听着——一只亮晶晶的眼睛先闭上，再睁开，另一只又闭上，然后再睁开——接着，它轻轻一跳，像一个念头那样，静悄悄地飞走了。

艾拉又睁开了眼睛。

光变得更柔和了——暖金色渐渐变成珍珠灰。洞外，萤火虫们眨巴眨巴亮起了小灯，像一盏盏浮着的小蜡烛，忽隐忽现地穿过柳条帘子。

水还在滴落。  
石头还在唱歌。  
“叮……咚……叮……”

艾拉长长地、慢慢地、轻轻地叹了一口气——像风吹过高高的草丛。

她把羊毛袜子往上拉了拉，盖住了脚踝。她用手抚平身下的青苔。她让肩膀一点点放松下来，沉甸甸的，又暖洋洋的。她的眼皮也热乎乎的，像黄油放在阳光底下，软软的，懒懒的。

她还不用急着回家呢。  
山洞抱着她。  
歌声抱着她。  
那颗小石头的水池也抱着她——温柔的，稳稳的，

于是她就留下来了，身子蜷成一小团，像卷心菜嫩芽在安静的光里慢慢舒展。水的歌声越来越轻——不是要消失，而是更深了，像摇篮曲慢慢沉进呼吸之间的那一小段宁静里。银亮亮的小水波，一圈圈绕着她光着的脚趾，凉凉的，柔柔的，每一道涟漪都哼着不同的调子：“叮……嘘……呜——呜……”，好像水池也在跟着她慢慢、轻轻吸气，一起呼吸呢。

莉莉望着池子正中央，一颗小石头——光滑得像月光擦亮的玻璃，颜色像暴风雨快要散开前的云——静静地躺在那儿。它没有沉下去，只是轻轻浮着，被水温柔地托在掌心里。莉莉看着看着，小石头忽然开始发光啦——不是亮晃晃的，也不是刺眼的，而是像黄昏刚来时，第一只萤火虫怯生生亮起的光：暖暖的，金灿灿的，软软的。

“它也在做梦吗？”她小声问。

山洞没有用话回答她。  
可就在那一眨眼的工夫，洞壁微微一闪——泛出柔柔的、珍珠母贝那样的光，像把贝母举到晨光里看。在这光里，莉莉没看见什么画，却感到了好多好多感觉：安全、归属、一种不需要理由的、静静的开心。就像夏天午后，新换上的干净床单；像最爱的杯子装着温温的牛奶；像被好好盖好被子，下巴暖暖的，脚丫子 snug snug 的，心里满满当当的。

一阵微风，凉凉的、甜甜的，像揉碎了的薄荷叶，从洞口悄悄飘进来——比一声叹息还要轻。它轻轻掀起莉莉几根头发，又温柔地拂过她的脸颊，像晚风送来的、一个软软的吻。洞外，世界正慢慢安静下来：小鸟收好了翅膀，钻进窝里；兔子缩进深深的洞穴；连蟋蟀也把叫声调成了迷迷糊糊的哼哼。整座森林屏住了呼吸——静静听着。

莉莉长长地、深深地、轻轻地叹了口气，然后松开一直搭在光滑岩沿上的小手。一根一根，她的手指慢慢松开——大拇指、小指头、中指……像傍晚时分，花瓣一朵一朵合拢。

她的手臂变重了，膝盖变软了，整个身体，一点点、一点点，陷进山洞地面那个刚刚好、软乎乎的青苔小窝里。

小石头水池的光，轻轻脉动了一下——慢，稳，像水底传来的心跳——随着这一下，莉莉的眼睫毛轻轻颤了颤，然后缓缓垂下，半遮着眼睛，长长的睫毛，黑黑的，在脸颊上投下温柔的影子。她没有跟睡意打架，也没有想刷牙、没想跟妈妈说晚安、也没想楼道的灯会不会一直亮着。她只觉得：山洞暖暖的安静，水唱的液体摇篮曲，身下青苔软软的托着她，还有那颗浮着的小石头，闪着暖暖的金光，像一颗小小的、不说话的星星，守着她呢。

一只蝙蝠从洞口飞过——不远，也不响——只是像一块丝绒做的影子，轻轻掠过紫莹莹的天空。莉莉没睁眼，嘴角却弯起了笑。她知道，这儿的蝙蝠一点儿也不可怕。它们是夜里的开花者，就像月下花，只在世界变得又软又静的时候，才悄悄打开自己。

她的呼吸越来越慢——更长，更深，更轻——每一次呼气，都像热茶上冒起的一缕白汽，轻轻散开。她的脚趾轻轻蜷了一下，就再也不动了。她的两只小手，现在摊开放在腿上，掌心朝上，变得暖暖的、沉沉的，好像里面装满了被阳光晒热的小河卵石。

水还在唱——可声音变得又慢又低，像远处的风，吹过高高的草丛。“嘘……咚……啊……”每一个音，都像一根细细的丝线，轻轻缠绕着她，一针一针，织成一张柔软的平静毯子。

她脑子里，只闪过明天的一小点念头——蒲公英绒球飘呀飘，水洼里映出彩虹，还有早晨阳光“哗啦”一下，淌满厨房餐桌的样子。可这念头没留下，像蒲公英种子一样，轻轻飘走了，没了影儿。

她的胸口——一起……一落……再一起……越来越慢……越来越慢……

山洞，陪着她一起呼吸。  
水池，稳稳地托着她。  
小石头，一直亮着——软软的，稳稳的，忠实的——仿佛它早就知道，她一定会来，也一定会再来。

然后，就在最后一道夕阳的光，悄悄融进树梢上方的深靛蓝时，莉莉——轻轻的，完完全全地——滑进了那片深深、静静的睡眠大海。

没有梦急急忙忙冲进来，也没有念头翻来滚去。只有一片安宁——宽宽的，暖暖的，不用说话的安宁——像羽毛一样轻软，像大树的根扎进肥沃泥土一样深沉。

洞外，星星一颗一颗，慢慢亮了起来。

洞里，在小石头水池山洞里，水还在唱着——轻轻的，更轻的，最轻的——它的声音像雾气一样，一圈圈绕着熟睡的孩子，把她抱得紧紧的，守得牢牢的，直到清晨的第一抹羞涩淡金，轻轻染亮天空。

而莉莉呢？  
莉莉睡着了。  
睡得深深的。  
睡得安安的。  
她心里，也悄悄唱着一支歌——在她最最安静的那个角落，唱着水教给她的、那支又慢又甜的摇篮曲——  
一支用涟漪写成的歌，  
一支用小石头低语的歌，  
一支，寂静本身在轻轻唱的歌。

她的呼吸，慢而稳，  
她的手指，静静的，暖暖的，  
她的心，跳着
contentEn:
Once, deep in the heart of the Willow-Wind Woods—where the trees leaned low to whisper secrets to the breeze and fireflies drifted like slow, golden stars—there lived a small child named Elara. Elara wore soft wool socks with one blue toe and one green, and she carried a cloth satchel stitched with daisies. She did not rush. She did not shout. She liked best the quiet times—the hush between raindrops, the sigh of a sleeping cat, the way dust motes danced in a sunbeam just before bedtime.

One evening, when the sky turned the color of warm honey and the crickets began their soft, steady hum, Elara followed a narrow path made of mossy stones and shy violets. The path wound downward, gently, like a sleepy river finding its way home. Her bare feet felt cool earth, smooth pebbles, and velvety moss—all soft as kitten ears.

And then—oh!—she heard it.

A sound like water humming a lullaby.

Not loud. Not fast. Just *shhh-ooom… shhh-ooom…* like breath and bubbles, like a song half-remembered from a dream.

Elara stopped. She tilted her head. A ladybug landed on her nose and stayed there, tiny legs tickling, wings folded like folded silk.

The sound came from behind a curtain of weeping willow branches—long, slender leaves swaying low, brushing the ground like green fingers. Elara parted them, ever so gently, and stepped through.

There, nestled in the hillside like a secret the earth had tucked away, was a cave.

But not a dark or shadowy cave—not at all.

This cave opened wide and kind, its mouth rimmed with smooth, round stones worn soft by time and water. Sunlight still spilled in, warm and golden, catching the sparkle of a little pool right at the cave’s heart. The pool was no bigger than a soup bowl—and yet it sang.

It wasn’t the water *in* the pool that sang. It was the water *falling into* it.

From a high ledge above, a thin, silver thread of water slipped down—a trickle, really—just a ribbon of clear, cool light. And as it fell, it struck a single, perfect pebble resting on the ledge’s edge.

*Plink.*

Then another drop fell.

*Plonk.*

Then another.

*Plink… plonk… plink…*

Each drop landed just so, tapping the pebble like a tiny finger on a tiny drum. And the pebble—smooth and gray with speckles of rose quartz—gave back a soft, round note. Not sharp. Not loud. Just *warm*, like a hug in sound.

Elara sat cross-legged on the mossy floor, her daisy-satchel beside her. She watched the water fall. She watched the pebble catch each drop. She watched the ripples spread across the pool—tiny circles, one inside the next, never hurrying, never stopping.

A white moth fluttered in, wings like folded parchment, and settled on the edge of the pool. It didn’t drink. It simply rested, its wings rising and falling with the same gentle rhythm as the water’s song.

Elara closed her eyes.

She heard the *plink-plonk* like a heartbeat—slow, sure, steady.

She felt the cave’s warmth around her, like being wrapped in a quilt of quiet.

She smelled damp stone and wild mint growing near the entrance, and the faint, sweet scent of woodruff—low and green and sleepy.

She thought of her grandmother’s hands, kneading dough on a flour-dusted table.  
She thought of the way clouds softened at sunset, turning peach and lavender.  
She thought of how her own breath slowed when she lay on her back in the clover, watching the sky turn from blue to dusky rose.

Inside the cave, time didn’t tick or race. It *glowed*. Like honey left in the sun.

Elara reached out—not to touch the water, not to move the pebble—but just to hold her hand near the pool’s edge, where mist rose in soft, silver wisps. The mist curled around her fingers, cool and kind, and vanished like a whispered word.

A robin hopped to the cave mouth and tilted its head. It didn’t sing. It simply listened—with one bright eye closed, then the other—before hopping away, silent as a thought.

Elara opened her eyes again.

The light had grown softer now—pale gold giving way to pearl-gray. Fireflies blinked awake outside, drifting in and out of the willow curtain like floating candles.

The water still fell.

The pebble still sang.

*Plink… plonk… plink…*

Elara sighed—a long, slow, soft sigh, like wind through tall grass.

She pulled her wool socks up over her ankles. She smoothed the moss beneath her. She let her shoulders settle, heavy and happy. Her eyelids grew warm, like butter left in the sun.

She didn’t need to go home just yet.  
The cave held her.  
The song held her.  
The pebble-pool held her—gentle, steady,

and so she stayed, curled like a fiddlehead fern unfurling in quiet light. The water’s song softened further—not fading, but deepening, like a lullaby sinking into the hush between breaths. Tiny silver ripples swirled around her bare toes, cool and kind, each one humming a different note: *plink… shhh… mur-mur…* as if the pool were breathing in time with her own slow, soft inhales.

Lily watched a single pebble—smooth as moon-polished glass, the colour of storm-clouds just before they part—rest at the very centre of the pool. It didn’t sink. It floated, barely, cradled by the water’s gentle hold. And as she watched, the pebble began to glow—not bright, not sharp, but like the first shy gleam of firefly light at dusk: warm, golden, tender.

“Is it dreaming too?” she whispered.

The cave didn’t answer with words. Instead, the walls shimmered—just for a heartbeat—with soft, pearlescent light, like mother-of-pearl held up to dawn. And in that shimmer, Lily saw not pictures, but feelings: safety. Belonging. A quiet joy that needed no reason. It was the feeling of clean sheets on a summer afternoon, of warm milk in a favourite cup, of being tucked in just so—chin covered, toes snug, heart full.

A breeze, cool and sweet as crushed mint, drifted in from the cave’s mouth—no louder than a sigh. It lifted a few strands of Lily’s hair and carried them softly across her cheek, like a kiss from the evening air. Outside, the world was settling: birds had folded their wings into nests, rabbits nestled deep in burrows, even the crickets had lowered their chirping to a drowsy hum. The forest held its breath—and listened.

Lily sighed, long and low, and let her fingers uncurl from where they’d been resting on the smooth stone ledge. One by one, her fingers relaxed—the thumb, the pinkie, the middle finger, like petals closing at twilight. Her arms grew heavier, her knees softer, her whole body sinking deeper into the mossy hollow where the cave floor curved just right to hold her.

The pebble-pool’s light pulsed once—slow, steady, like a heartbeat under water—and with it, Lily’s eyelids fluttered, then settled, half-lowered, lashes dark against her cheeks. She didn’t fight the sleep. She didn’t think about brushing teeth or saying goodnight to Mama or whether the hallway light would stay on. There was only this: the cave’s warm hush, the water’s liquid lullaby, the soft press of moss beneath her, and the gentle, golden gleam of the floating pebble, watching over her like a tiny, silent star.

A bat flitted past the cave mouth—not near, not loud—just a velvet shadow gliding across the violet sky. Lily smiled without opening her eyes. She knew bats weren’t scary here. They were night-bloomers, like moonflowers, opening only when the world grew soft and still.

Her breathing slowed—longer, deeper, quieter—each exhale a soft release, like steam rising from warm tea. Her toes curled just once, then stilled. Her hands, now resting palm-up on her lap, grew warm and heavy, as if filled with sun-warmed river stones.

The water sang on—but now the notes were slower, lower, like distant wind through tall grass. *Shhh… plonk… ah…* Each sound wrapped around her like a silken thread, weaving a blanket of calm, stitch by gentle stitch.

She thought—just for a breath—of tomorrow: of dandelion fluff drifting, of rainbows in puddles, of the way sunlight spilled across the kitchen table at breakfast. But the thought didn’t linger. It floated away, light as thistledown, and was gone.

Her chest rose… and fell… and rose again… slower… slower…

The cave breathed with her.

The pool held her.

The pebble glowed—soft, constant, faithful—as if it had always known she would come, and always would return.

And then, just as the last stripe of sunset bled into indigo above the trees, Lily slipped—so gently, so completely—into the deep, quiet sea of sleep.

No dreams rushed in. No thoughts tumbled. Just peace—wide and warm and wordless—as soft as down, as deep as roots in rich earth.

Outside, the stars blinked awake, one by one.

Inside the Pebble-Pool Cave, the water kept singing—soft, soft, softer—its voice curling like mist around the sleeping child, holding her close, keeping watch, until morning’s first blush painted the sky pale gold.

And Lily?  
Lily slept.  
Deep.  
Safe.  
Singing inside, in the quietest part of her, the same slow, sweet song the water had taught her—  
a lullaby written in ripples,  
whispered in pebbles,  
sung by the stillness itself.  

Her breath, slow and sure,  
her fingers still and warm,  
her heart beating
